events.text: Where The Covenant with Noah ended: Noah (cast, older) on the mountainside in Ararat pressing a vine cutting into turned earth. Years later: the same slope covered in rows of vines heavy with dark grapes in late summer light, the family (cast) small among the rows, seen from behind, cutting the clusters into baskets.
The first vintage. Baskets of grapes, bare feet treading in a stone press, juice running dark into a jar. A low warm pulse.

Montage, quick, each shot its own, the pulse slowing: a clay cup filled from a jar by lamplight; Noah's face close, tired and smiling, the cup at his lips; the tent flap falling shut; the lamp inside guttering; the cup on its side on the rug, wine spilled; Ham (cast) at the tent door seen from behind, light spilling out past him; Shem and Japheth (cast) walking backward, a cloak across their shoulders, their faces turned away.
Morning. Noah (cast, older), his face close, waking under a cloak inside the tent, the light through the hide hard and white, his eyes slowly understanding.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.
Noah's face. Cut to black and silence on the last second.

The picture follows each question. Noah's empty cup lying on its side on a rug in a dim tent. The tent door seen from outside at night, the lamp glowing through the hide, a man's shadow standing in it. A small boy seen from behind, holding his father's hand on a hillside. An old book of the nations open by candlelight, and beside it a pair of iron shackles lying open and empty on rough planks.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Why does the man who survived the flood end up drunk in his tent? What did Ham actually do? Why is Canaan cursed, when Ham did the wrong? And how was this chapter twisted to defend slavery? Four questions. Twelve verses.
NOAH'S SONS / Genesis 9:18 to 29
Title over the vineyard on the mountainside at dawn, mist in the rows. A low hit, then the wind.

The mountainside in the morning: Shem, Ham and Japheth (cast) walking up through the vines toward the camp, side by side, each face close in turn; one family, one skin, the same dark curled hair; Ham's wife (cast) behind them with a small boy, Canaan, holding her hand, seen from behind.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And Ham was the father of Canaan.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth was populated.
The three brothers at the top of the rows, the land wide below them. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Three names. And from them, the whole earth. Every people that will ever live is about to come from this one family. The next chapter will trace them, nation by nation.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: But listen to the line the narrator adds before anything has happened. And Ham was the father of Canaan. He will say it again in a moment. Canaan plays no part in the scene. The narrator is telling us to watch him.
The boy Canaan seen from behind at the edge of the camp, throwing pebbles down the slope; Ham's hand on his shoulder.
The boy's pebble skipping down the slope. Breath.
Noah (cast, older) kneeling among young vines, both hands whole in the frame, tying a shoot to a stake; his face close, the sun on it; the turned red earth around him.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Now Noah, a man of the soil, proceeded to plant a vineyard.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: A man of the soil. In Hebrew, ish ha'adamah. A man of the ground. Adamah is the ground Adam was taken from. The ground that was cursed. When Noah was born, his father Lamech named him in hope of relief from

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the ground that the LORD has cursed

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Now the ground gives its best gift. A vineyard.
Noah's hands on the vine. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The verb behind proceeded to is chalal. To begin. And in these chapters that verb keeps opening new beginnings that go wrong. Before the flood,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: when men began to multiply

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: After it, Nimrod

events.speaker: READER
events.text: began to be a mighty one

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And at Babel,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: if they have begun to do this

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Every fresh start in the early world carries the seeds of new trouble.

Set piece: the first vintage, no narration. Each shot its own: grapes heavy and dusty on the vine; the family (cast) cutting clusters into baskets, hands whole and level; the boy Canaan carrying a small basket, seen from behind; Japheth (cast) and Shem's wife (cast) treading grapes in a stone press, their long robes held clear of the juice and falling below the knee, laughing; juice running down a channel into a clay jar; the jar sealed with clay. The warm theme of the camp, rising.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Wine was for feasts and offerings across the ancient world. Scripture can praise

events.speaker: READER
events.text: wine that gladdens the heart of man

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: and it can warn that

events.speaker: READER
events.text: wine is a mocker

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: If Noah was the first to plant a vine, he may not have known what it could do. The text does not excuse him. And it does not lecture him either. It simply tells us what happened.
The sealed jars in the shade of the tent. Breath.

Evening at the camp: Noah (cast, older) sitting alone at the door of his tent, a clay cup in his hand, filling it again from a jar; his face close, warm in the lamplight, his eyes heavy. Then he rises unsteadily and goes inside, and the tent flap falls shut behind him.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: But when he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and uncovered himself inside his tent.
The tent from outside in the dark, the lamp glowing through the hide and slowly dimming. The wind. No music.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: So why does the righteous man end the story drunk in his tent? Because the flood had not solved the human problem. This is Noah who

events.speaker: READER
events.text: walked with God

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Saved from judgment. Blessed with the words of creation. And within a few verses of the covenant, he falls into shame. The new world is not an innocent world.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: God had said it before the rain had dried. He would never again destroy the earth,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The flood cleaned the world. It could not clean the heart.
The dim tent. Breath.

Remembered from The Fall: the tree in the garden, a hand closing on its fruit; the man and the woman seen from behind among the trees, holding fig leaves to themselves; then God's provision, the garments of skin lying folded on a stone.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Listen to the pattern. A man of the ground plants, as God planted a garden. The fruit is taken and consumed. Nakedness is exposed. Shame follows. A garment covers it. A knowing comes afterward. And the scene ends in curse and blessing.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The second father of humanity repeats the failure of the first. A new start from inside the old humanity, even one led by a righteous man, cannot make a clean world.
The garments of skin on the stone, then the tent at night. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Uncovered himself. The verb is galah, to uncover, to expose, and here its form turns back on Noah. He is the one who exposed himself.

Night. Ham (cast) coming up from the flock with a lamp, stopping at his father's tent; the flap blown half open by the wind; Ham seen only from behind in the doorway, the lamplight falling past him into the tent; nothing inside shown. Then his face, close, lit from below, staring.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers outside.
Ham (cast) walking quickly to the fire where Shem and Japheth (cast) sit; Ham talking, his hand gesturing back toward the tent; the brothers' faces close, one after the other, changing.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Nakedness. Ervah. It means more than an unclothed body. It carries shame and disgrace. And there is the narrator's second warning. Ham, the father of Canaan.
The fire, the brothers silent. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: So what did Ham actually do? The text says only two things. He saw, and he told. Most readers through history have taken that plainly. The looking itself was the offence, and he made it worse by spreading it. In a culture of honour and shame, that was contempt for a father.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Others note that in Leviticus, seeing or uncovering nakedness is a way of speaking of a sexual act, and suggest something worse happened in that tent.
The tent in the dark, the flap moving in the wind. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: But the text says Noah uncovered himself, and the brothers put it right with a garment. That fits a sin of looking and exposing. Shameful, but no more than the words say. Either way, Ham dishonoured his father, and did it in the open.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The prophet Habakkuk links wine and exposure the same way. He pronounces woe on the one who gives his neighbours drink,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: in order to gaze at their nakedness
Ham's face in the firelight, then turning away. Breath.
Shem and Japheth (cast) rising from the fire without a word; Shem lifting a heavy woven cloak from a peg by the fire, both hands whole in the frame.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Then Shem and Japheth took a garment and placed it across their shoulders, and walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away so that they did not see their father’s nakedness.

Set piece: the covering, no narration, slow, each step its own shot. The two brothers spreading the cloak between them across their shoulders; turning their backs to the tent door; walking backward step by careful step, their bare feet on the rug; their faces turned aside and close, eyes shut; the cloak lowering out of frame below their shoulders; the lamp; then the two walking out into the night without looking back. Nothing of Noah shown. A single held string note.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Watch how slowly the narrator tells it. Ham saw and told. Two verbs. His brothers took the garment, placed it, walked backward, covered their father, and did not see. Almost frame by frame. Their refusal to look stands out against his looking.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Three times in two verses, the narrator names the father's nakedness. And the garment has the article in Hebrew. The garment. As if one particular cloak was at hand. They covered him without a second look.
The two brothers outside the tent in the dark, saying nothing. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Ham exposes. His brothers cover. Ham tells. They act without a word. It is a lesson in how to treat someone else's failure.

The wilderness camp at the foot of Sinai, the mountain dark with cloud behind it: the brick-maker (cast), chest up, standing among the people listening, his old father (seen from behind, bent, white haired, leaning on a staff) beside him; the brick-maker's hand under his father's arm.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The brick-maker heard the weight of this at Sinai. The fifth commandment.

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: Honor your father and mother

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Israel's law made it a capital crime to strike or curse a parent, and Moses pronounced a curse on

events.speaker: READER
events.text: he who dishonors his father or mother

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: This was not only good manners. It reflects God's own order. The Son honours the Father.
The brick-maker steadying his father as the people sit. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: What carries forward from this scene is clear. A warning against drunkenness. Paul writes,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The command to honour parents. And the call to cover the failings of others, not to broadcast them. The New Testament puts it simply. Love covers a multitude of sins.
The cloak over the sleeping figure, seen only as a dark shape from the doorway. Breath.

Morning in the tent: Noah (cast, older) waking under the heavy cloak, his face close; he sits up slowly, pulls the cloak round him, sees the cup on its side, the spilled wine dark on the rug. Then at the tent door, Shem (cast) standing with his eyes lowered.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: When Noah awoke from his drunkenness and learned what his youngest son had done to him,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: he said, “Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.”
Noah's face, close, very still. Silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: These are the only words Noah ever speaks in Scripture. And they are a curse and a blessing.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: A servant of servants. Ebed abadim. It is the Hebrew way of saying the most. Like holy of holies, the most holy place. Servant of servants means the lowest servant of all.
Shem at the tent door, his eyes lowered. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: So why is Canaan cursed, when Ham did the wrong? Some see a correspondence. A son wronged his father, so he is struck through his son. Some suggest Canaan took part, though the text does not say so.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: But the best answer is in the narrator's own signals. He flagged Canaan twice. The oracle is a prophecy. It looks ahead to the Canaanites Israel would meet, a people whose conduct would come to match their forefather's sin.
The boy Canaan, seen from behind, asleep by the fire's ashes. Breath.
The wilderness camp on the plains across the Jordan at evening: the brick-maker (cast), chest up, looking west across the river to the hills of Canaan, his wife and sons beside him seen from behind.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: For the brick-maker, Canaan was not an idea. It was the land across the river. God warned Israel that its peoples had defiled the land, and that Israel held no immunity. If they copied Canaan, the land would cast them out too.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And the judgment did not come in haste. God told Abram

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The curse waited for centuries, until their own sin had filled up. Scripture insists that each person answers for their own sin.
Gibeon, later: men of a Canaanite town carrying bundles of wood and water jars up a stony path toward the camp of Israel, seen from behind.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Israel's first hearers saw the oracle at work in their own history. Canaanite towns were put to forced labour. The Gibeonites became

events.speaker: READER
events.text: woodcutters and water carriers
The water carriers on the path. Breath.
A dim study by candlelight: a heavy old book lying open, a quill beside it; then a pair of iron shackles lying open and empty on weathered planks by the sea, the light cold.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Now the fourth question. For centuries, some claimed a curse of Ham to justify the enslavement of Africans. It is one of the worst misuses of the Bible in history.
The empty shackles. Silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And the text gives it no ground. Read it again. Ham is not cursed. Canaan is. The Canaanites lived in the land between Egypt and Syria. And the sons of Ham usually linked with Africa, Cush, Mizraim and Put, are not cursed at all.

Graphic, gold on dark stone: three names, SHEM, HAM, JAPHETH; under HAM four names branch out, CUSH, MIZRAIM, PUT, CANAAN; only CANAAN is marked, and the line under it runs on into the land between the river of Egypt and the hills of Syria on a faint map.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Noah's words are a prophecy of what would come of these lines. They are not a command to anyone to enslave anyone. And servant of servants is not a comment on the worth of any people before God.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Any reading that turns this oracle into a ranking of races abuses the text. Shem, Ham and Japheth were brothers. One family. And every nation on earth comes from them.
Faces, close, one after another, all of one family: Shem, Ham, Japheth, their wives. No music.

Outside the tent in the morning: Noah (cast, older) standing, the cloak round his shoulders, Shem and Japheth (cast) before him with their heads bowed, Noah's hand on Shem's head; Noah's face close as he speaks.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: He also declared: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem! May Canaan be the servant of Shem.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: May God expand the territory of Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his servant.”
Noah's hand lifting from Shem's head. The wind. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Listen to what Noah blesses. Not Shem. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem. Barak. To speak good over someone. The blessing lies in whom Shem has as his God.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And this is the only place in the oracle where the covenant name appears. The LORD. It is joined to Shem. For Japheth, Noah says simply, God.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Shem means name. In two chapters, the builders of Babel will say, let us

events.speaker: READER
events.text: make a name for ourselves

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And God will say to Abram, Shem's descendant,

events.speaker: GOD
events.text: I will make your name great

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The blessing of the God of Shem becomes the blessing of the God of Abraham.
Shem's face, close, lifting. Breath.
Japheth (cast) standing on a ridge at dawn looking out over a vast land of hills and far coasts; then the same dawn on the camp below, the tents of Shem in a row, smoke rising.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Then Japheth. May God expand. In Hebrew, yapht. It sounds like his name, yepheth. Both names carry their future. Japheth will be enlarged. Shem will bear the name of God.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: But who will dwell in the tents of Shem? Some read it as God Himself, making His presence live among Shem's descendants. Most translations read it as Japheth, coming to share in Shem's blessing.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The two are not far apart. If God dwells in Shem's tents, and Japheth comes to live there, both point to one hope. The nations joining the people among whom God has chosen to live.
Japheth walking down toward the tents. Breath.

Many years on: the vineyard terraces spread wide across the mountainside, the camp grown into a settlement of tents and stone pens; children and grandchildren among the vines, seen from behind; Noah (cast, older), his hair white, sitting at his tent door watching them, his face close.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: After the flood, Noah lived 350 years.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: So Noah lived a total of 950 years, and then he died.
A lamp burning low inside the tent, then out. Noah's three sons (cast), now grey, standing at a cairn of stones on the slope, seen from behind. The wind. Silence.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Nine hundred and fifty years. And then he died. It is the refrain of Genesis five. Adam lived, and then he died. Noah's entry in that list began before the flood and was left open through the whole flood story. Now it is closed. The man who came through the waters still goes the way of Adam.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And notice what God does not do. The family He rescued fell into sin almost at once. And He sent no flood. His covenant faithfulness does not depend on ours.
The cairn on the slope, the vineyard below. Breath.

Set piece: the three sons go out, no narration. Each its own shot from the mountainside: Japheth's family with their flocks walking north and west along a ridge toward far coasts; Ham's family going south down a valley toward the river plains, the boy Canaan, grown now, walking among them; Shem's family staying among the tents of the highlands, smoke rising. All seen from behind. A wide, rising theme.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: God is sovereign over history. The oracle was spoken by a man who had failed, and it came to pass. God works through broken families to steer history toward His purpose.
The three families small in the wide land. Breath.

Remembered from The Fall and from the vineyard: the hand on the fruit; the cup on its side in the tent. Then a road in Galilee at dusk, a man in a seamless robe seen only from straight behind, His warm olive brown skin and thick black curly hair, walking alone; no part of His face shown.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Noah was set up as a second Adam. The father of a new humanity, blessed with Adam's words, a man of the ground. And like Adam, he fell. A new humanity needs a new head. Paul calls Christ

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the last Adam

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Where Noah failed, and a son shamed his father, here is the faithful Son. Jesus said of His Father,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: I always do what pleases Him
The figure on the road at dusk. Breath.
The hill outside the city under a dark sky: at the foot of the three posts, far off, no figures; close on soldiers' hands on the ground casting lots over a seamless robe spread on the stones.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Ham exposed his father's shame. Shem and Japheth covered it without looking. Christ went further than either. He did not look away from our shame. He took it on Himself. At the cross He was stripped, and soldiers divided His garments. He endured the cross,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: scorning its shame

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: so that the naked might be clothed. Paul writes,

events.speaker: READER
events.text: all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ
The robe on the stones. Breath.
A long scroll unrolling on a table by lamplight, a column of names in faint ink; then the hills of Judah at night, a small town below with a few lamps lit.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And the blessing on the God of Shem runs on. Shem's line goes to Abram, to Israel, to David. Luke traces Jesus back to

events.speaker: READER
events.text: the son of Shem, the son of Noah

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The blessing announced in a tent after the flood reaches its goal in the one born in Bethlehem. And the tents? John says

events.speaker: READER
events.text: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: A word that recalls pitching a tent. And the Gentiles, the far nations, are brought in. Paul calls them

events.speaker: READER
events.text: no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints
The lamps of the town. Breath.
A woman of Canaan, her head covered, kneeling on a dusty road, seen from behind; the hem of a seamless robe and a man's sandalled feet stopping before her.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: And the curse? Christ

events.speaker: READER
events.text: redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: In Christ there is no permanent class of the cursed. Rahab of Jericho, a Canaanite, was saved and became an ancestor of Christ. And a Canaanite woman once begged Jesus for her daughter. He praised her great faith and granted what she asked. Mercy, from the son of Shem, to the line of Canaan.
The woman lifting her head. Breath.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: One care. The vineyard and the wine are not hidden pictures of the Lord's Supper. The links rest on the New Testament's own themes. The last Adam. The bearing of shame. The blessing of the nations.
High bright light and a great crowd seen from behind, dressed in white, of every nation, filling the frame; no throne and no figure above them.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: At the end of the story, the people of God are dressed in white. The nations that came from Shem, Ham and Japheth are one family before the throne. And the curse that began with the ground is lifted.

events.speaker: READER
events.text: No longer will there be any curse
The crowd in white, the light growing. The warm chord. No narration.

Evening in the wilderness camp: the brick-maker (cast), chest up, coming into his tent; his old father asleep on a mat, seen from behind; the brick-maker lifting his own cloak from his shoulders, both hands whole in the frame, and laying it gently over his father; his face close, tender.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: The brick-maker's father was old, and he had failed in his time, like every father. The story of Noah's sons taught Israel what kind of people to be. People who honour father and mother. People who cover shame instead of spreading it.
The cloak settling over the sleeping father. Soft.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Ham exposed his father's shame. His brothers covered it. When you learn something embarrassing about someone, which brother are you more like?
The brick-maker sitting down beside his father in the lamplight. The camp quiet outside.
The mountainside in Ararat at dawn, empty: the old vineyard gone wild on the terraces; three paths leading away from it, north, south and east, into a vast land.

events.speaker: GUIDE
events.text: Three sons. Three paths across the earth. Next, Genesis names their children, nation by nation. And every one of them is family.
The three paths in the dawn light, the wind over the terraces. Then quiet.
